title: Control Rights and Capital Structure: An Empirical Investigation
research_question: How do incentive conflicts between firms and their creditors, and the associated transfer of control rights to creditors after poor performance, affect corporate debt policy and capital structure decisions? Specifically, do creditor interventions following breaches of financial covenants cause persistent changes in net debt issuance and leverage, and is this effect stronger when borrowers have limited access to alternative financing?
data_description: The primary data set is a quarterly panel of nonfinancial U.S. publicly listed firms drawn from Compustat covering 1996 to 2005, yielding 135,736 firm-quarter observations on 6,381 firms. The authors hand-collect financial covenant violations directly from 10-K and 10-Q SEC filings using a Perl-based search of 20 violation-related phrases, exploiting Regulation S-X disclosure requirements. Each firm-quarter is coded as in violation or not. Key outcome variables include net debt issuance and net equity issuance (scaled by lagged assets) and book leverage. Control variables include the accounting ratios on which covenants are commonly written (debt/assets, net worth, cash, EBITDA, cash flow, net income, interest expense, and interactions), plus firm size, tangibility, market-to-book, and an S&P rating indicator. A supplementary subsample uses 3,603 private credit agreements from DealScan with known covenant thresholds, and a random sample of 500 violators is read in detail to identify creditor actions.
institutional_context: Private credit agreements between U.S. corporations and lenders typically include financial covenants—maintenance tests on accounting ratios such as debt-to-EBITDA, coverage ratios, net worth, and liquidity—that the borrower must satisfy each reporting period. When a borrower breaches such a covenant, contractual provisions grant creditors the right to immediately accelerate outstanding balances and terminate any unused portion of revolving credit facilities. In practice, lenders rarely call the loan; instead, they use these rights as bargaining leverage to renegotiate terms, often reducing credit availability, raising interest spreads, demanding additional collateral, or imposing reporting and investment restrictions. SEC Regulation S-X requires firms to disclose unresolved covenant breaches in their 10-K and 10-Q filings, making violations observable. Over a quarter of public firms experience such a breach during 1996–2005, and violations occur far more frequently than payment defaults, even among investment-grade borrowers, making them a pervasive channel through which creditors influence borrower behavior outside of formal bankruptcy.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = firms violating covenants, control = firms not violating covenants; cutoff = covenant violation threshold

key_variables.control: firms that have not violated financial covenants

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The study finds that an increase in creditor control rights due to covenant violations leads to a decrease in firm financial leverage.
